(i) we have compared the gene expressions of WT and KO mice in three regions (cortex, cerebellum and midbrain) by using microarray; (ii) we have confirmed the results by real-time PCR; (iii) we have identified new genes that could play a role in RTT, and (iv) we have identified a new mechanism for the involvement of MeCP2 in the regulation of the gene expression.

the gene expression profiles in three regions of brain from Mecp2-Null mice compared to wild type mice revealed seven direct targets of Mecp2 and three overexpressing genes due to an in direct effect.
we identified new target genes of the protein methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 in the mouse cortex, midbrain and cerebellum.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of genes that could be involved in the pathogenesis of Rett syndrome and could be used as new targets for therapeutic intervention.
the identification of new target genes regulated in vivo by MeCP2, and the characterization of the mechanisms that regulate their expression.
the identification of new target genes regulated in a mouse model for RTT and their possible involvement in the pathogenesis of this disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our study has identified new neuronal targets of MeCP 2 in the brain of mice that are excellent candidates for involvement in various aspects of RTT.
the results of this study are a significant step forward for the comprehension of the molecular mechanisms of the disease, and that they will help to design future therapies.
MeCP2 is an epigenetic modulator that regulates the expression of a number of genes in the brain, and the absence of this protein in mice causes a complex neurological phenotype.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified new genes that might be involved in the pathogenesis of RTT, thus opening new perspectives for the development of therapeutic strategies for RTT.
the MeCP2 protein is a key factor for the normal function of the nervous system and that its dysfunction leads to a variety of neurological diseases.

The main takeaway from our work is that
MeCP2 is a key regulator of gene expression in the brain, and that its absence leads to the overexpression of genes that are directly or indirectly bound by MeCP2 in the brain.
we have identified several new genes that are regulated by MeCP2 in the mouse brain and that could be involved in the pathology of RTT.

the lack of Mecp-2 in neurons leads to the overexpression of a set of genes involved in the regulation of neuronal excitability, synaptic plasticity, and neuronal survival, which are all processes that are impaired in the disease.
